newsitem.title: FRANCE: French welfare system remains deep in the red.
newsitem.headline: French welfare system remains deep in the red.

text.p: The French government pledged on Monday higher taxes and cost curbs would reduce deficits in the welfare system, which has run deep into the red less than a year after a big debt write-off meant to put it back on its feet.

The independent social security accounts commission said the welfare deficit would reach 51.6 billion francs this year -- by far overshooting a government target of 17 billion francs -- but down from 67.4 billion francs last year.
It warned that the deficit would reach 47.15 billion next year if no new measures were taken.

Labour Minister Jacques Barrot told a news conference however that new measures, including higher excise duties on alcohol and tobacco, a reform to payroll charges and spending curbs, would bring the deficit to 29.7 billion next year.
"Between the forecast and the 29.7 billion francs, there is a margin in which political will must intervene," Barrot, who will present a welfare bill to parliament next month, said.

The social security system -- which uses mostly payroll charges to fund healthcare, pensions and family benefits -- is run separately from the central government budget and has long been the weak link in efforts to reduce France's public deficit.

Founded in 1945 and co-managed by the employers' federation and trade unions, it has defied in recent years all government attempts to restore it to balance as generous healthcare spending and high unemployment have eaten into revenues.
Earlier this year, the government carried out the second debt write-off in just over two years to lift the burden of paying debt service charges from the social security system.
It set up a new welfare debt repayment fund, CADES, to take on the debt and imposed a flat 0.5 percent tax on virtually all income, the RDS, to repay the debt.
But weak growth, which left unemployment at a record high of 12.5 percent, has wiped out all the gains from those changes.
Barrot said 90 percent of the deficit overshoot this year was due to a much lower than expected rise in total wages, from which payroll charges are deducted.
He also argued that if the government had not already taken strong action to curb healthcare spending, this year's deficit would be nearer 90 billion francs.
The Force Ouvriere trade union, however, blamed the government's austerity drive, saying it had squeezed economic growth and hit employment, reducing revenues for the welfare system.
It said it had long argued the problem was one of insufficient revenues rather than overspending.

"The priority given to the massive reduction of public deficits in order to meet Maastricht treaty criteria is creating serious problems for employment. It is not enough to be ready (for monetary union). We have to think about what state we will be in when we get there," it said in a statement.
Economists also questioned the credibility of the government's targets.
"The social security funding gap has been the Achilles' heel of French fiscal policy since 1993, and is likely to remain so next year," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.

Barrot stressed however the government's aim was to restore the welfare system to breakeven. He said there was no question of debt repayment fund CADES taking on extra debt to finance the new deficit as it was prevented by law from doing so.

State bank Caisse des Depots et Consignations and the French Treasury would ensure the welfare system's immediate cash flow needs were met and the government would review the situation in the spring, he said.
